claim: The phase of oscillations modulates neural activity representing categorical information using human intracranial recordings and high-frequency activity from local field potentials.
source: We previously demonstrated that the phase of oscillations modulates neural activity representing categorical information using human intracranial recordings and high-frequency activity from local field potentials (Watrous et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Watrous et al., 2015b).

claim: Phase-locked neural firing encodes information about a person's prospective navigational goal in the absence of firing rate changes.
source: Going beyond this work, using a novel oscillation detection algorithm, we identify phase-locked neural firing that encodes information about a person's prospective navigational goal in the absence of firing rate changes.
evidence: The claim is presented as a finding from the current study using a novel algorithm.

claim: Phase-coded neuronal firing is a component of the human neural code.
source: More generally, our findings identify phase-coded neuronal firing as a component of the human neural code.
evidence: The claim is based on the findings presented in the current study.

claim: Interactions between single-neuron spike timing and oscillations observed in the local field potential contribute to the neural code across species and behaviors.
source: In addition to the well-established role for behavior-related changes in neuronal firing rates, converging evidence across species and behaviors suggests that interactions between single-neuron spike timing and oscillations observed in the local field potential (LFP) also contribute to the neural code (Hyman et al., 2005; Huxter et al., 2003; Rutishauser et al., 2010; Belitski et al., 2008; Ng et al., 2013; Kayser et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Hippocampal and medial prefrontal cells in rodents show phase precession relative to theta oscillations during navigation.
source: In rodents, hippocampal and medial prefrontal cells show phase precession relative to theta oscillations during navigation (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Terada et al., 2017; Jones and Wilson, 2005), in which the theta phase of neuronal firing represents information about the animal's position (Jensen and Lisman, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior rodent studies.

claim: The theta phase of neuronal firing in rodents represents information about the animal's position.
source: In rodents, hippocampal and medial prefrontal cells show phase precession relative to theta oscillations during navigation (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Terada et al., 2017; Jones and Wilson, 2005), in which the theta phase of neuronal firing represents information about the animal's position (Jensen and Lisman, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Jensen and Lisman, 2000).

claim: Frequency-specific and phase-locked neuronal firing to low-frequency oscillations at different phases forms a basis of the human neural code according to SCERT.
source: For example, in Spectro-Contextual Encoding and Retrieval Theory (SCERT), we proposed that frequency-specific and phase-locked neuronal firing to low-frequency oscillations at different phases (i.e. phase coding) also forms a basis of the human neural code (Watrous and Ekstrom, 2014; Watrous et al., 2015b).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' theoretical model (SCERT) as described in cited prior work.

claim: High-frequency activity in the LFP can serve as a proxy for single-cell spiking.
source: We previously reported evidence for SCERT (Watrous et al., 2015a) using high-frequency activity in the LFP as a proxy for single-cell spiking (Crone et al., 1998; Manning et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The relationship between the spiking of particular single neurons and high-frequency activity in the human medial temporal lobe is complex and variable.
source: However, given the complex and variable relationship (Ekstrom et al., 2007; Manning et al., 2009; Rey et al., 2014) between the spiking of particular single neurons and high-frequency activity in the human medial temporal lobe (MTL), it is unclear whether human MTL neurons show phase coding of navigationally relevant information beyond an overall preference to fire at particular phases (Jacobs et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Human MTL neurons show an overall preference to fire at particular phases.
source: However, given the complex and variable relationship (Ekstrom et al., 2007; Manning et al., 2009; Rey et al., 2014) between the spiking of particular single neurons and high-frequency activity in the human medial temporal lobe (MTL), it is unclear whether human MTL neurons show phase coding of navigationally relevant information beyond an overall preference to fire at particular phases (Jacobs et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Jacobs et al., 2007).

claim: Activity in the human MTL and medial prefrontal cortex forms active representations of spatial context such as navigational goals.
source: Human imaging and lesion evidence indicate that activity in the human MTL and medial prefrontal cortex forms active representations of spatial context such as navigational goals (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Brown et al., 2016; Ciaramelli, 2008; Spiers and Maguire, 2007; Wolbers et al., 2007) in support of navigational planning (Horner et al., 2016; Bellmund et al., 2016; Kaplan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior imaging and lesion studies.

claim: Human MTL and medial prefrontal cortex support navigational planning.
source: Human imaging and lesion evidence indicate that activity in the human MTL and medial prefrontal cortex forms active representations of spatial context such as navigational goals (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Brown et al., 2016; Ciaramelli, 2008; Spiers and Maguire, 2007; Wolbers et al., 2007) in support of navigational planning (Horner et al., 2016; Bellmund et al., 2016; Kaplan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Neurons in the human MTL increase their firing rate when viewing goal locations.
source: Analyzing human single-neuron recordings from the MTL, previous studies have identified neurons that increase their firing rate when viewing goal locations (Ekstrom et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Ekstrom et al., 2003).

claim: Phase coding is a distinct phenomenon compared to rate coding in rodents.
source: It is also unknown whether rate and phase-coding co-exist in humans, as suggested by rodent studies that indicated that phase coding was a distinct phenomenon compared to rate coding (Huxter et al., 2003; Hyman et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: Spatial contextual representations for specific navigational goals are implemented by distinctive patterns of phase coding by individual neurons.
source: Drawing upon the phase-coding hypotheses from SCERT and related findings in rodents (Hollup et al., 2001; Hok et al., 2007; Hyman et al., 2005; O'Neill et al., 2013), we hypothesized that spatial contextual representations for specific navigational goals would be implemented by distinctive patterns of phase coding by individual neurons.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis based on SCERT and rodent findings.

claim: Medial temporal lobe structures and frontal cortex are implicated in navigational planning in rodents and humans.
source: Moreover, based on rodent (Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015) and human studies (Viard et al., 2011; Howard et al., 2014; Brown et al., 2016; Horner et al., 2016; Bellmund et al., 2016) implicating medial temporal lobe structures and frontal cortex in navigational planning, we reasoned that spike-phase coding may support these behaviors at the single-neuron level, hypothesizing that distinctive spike phase patterns would correspond to the neural network states representing planning and searching for particular goals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to rodent and human studies.

claim: Distinctive spike phase patterns correspond to neural network states representing planning and searching for particular goals.
source: Moreover, based on rodent (Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015) and human studies (Viard et al., 2011; Howard et al., 2014; Brown et al., 2016; Horner et al., 2016; Bellmund et al., 2016) implicating medial temporal lobe structures and frontal cortex in navigational planning, we reasoned that spike-phase coding may support these behaviors at the single-neuron level, hypothesizing that distinctive spike phase patterns would correspond to the neural network states representing planning and searching for particular goals.
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis based on prior rodent and human studies.

claim: Oscillatory frequencies should match between encoding and retrieval according to SCERT.
source: SCERT generally predicts that oscillatory frequencies should match between encoding and retrieval and that phase coding should occur at the dominant oscillatory frequency that occurs in a particular behavior and brain region.
evidence: The claim is a prediction from the SCERT theoretical model.

claim: Phase coding should occur at the dominant oscillatory frequency that occurs in a particular behavior and brain region according to SCERT.
source: SCERT generally predicts that oscillatory frequencies should match between encoding and retrieval and that phase coding should occur at the dominant oscillatory frequency that occurs in a particular behavior and brain region.
evidence: The claim is a prediction from the SCERT theoretical model.

claim: Hippocampal slow-theta oscillations are the most prominent during human virtual navigation.
source: Thus, based on the body of evidence indicating hippocampal slow-theta oscillations are the most prominent during human virtual navigation (Ekstrom et al., 2005; Watrous et al., 2011; Jacobs, 2014; Bush et al., 2017), we predicted here that phase coding should occur primarily at slow theta frequencies.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Phase coding should occur primarily at slow theta frequencies during human virtual navigation.
source: Thus, based on the body of evidence indicating hippocampal slow-theta oscillations are the most prominent during human virtual navigation (Ekstrom et al., 2005; Watrous et al., 2011; Jacobs, 2014; Bush et al., 2017), we predicted here that phase coding should occur primarily at slow theta frequencies.
evidence: The claim is presented as a prediction based on prior evidence.

claim: Driving time between stores significantly decreased throughout the task session.
source: Driving time between stores significantly decreased throughout the task session (Kruskal-Wallis test across sessions, p=0.007), indicating that the patients successfully learned the environment and planned efficient paths between stores.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.007) of behavioral data.

claim: Patients successfully learned the environment and planned efficient paths between stores.
source: Driving time between stores significantly decreased throughout the task session (Kruskal-Wallis test across sessions, p=0.007), indicating that the patients successfully learned the environment and planned efficient paths between stores.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing decreased driving time.

claim: 53 goal-responsive cells (11% of 466 MTL neurons) were identified with a main effect of goal (p<0.05).
source: We identified 53 such goal-responsive cells (11% of 466 MTL neurons; main effect of goal, p<0.05), which were present in 11 of 12 patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of neuronal firing data.

claim: Goal-responsive neurons were present in 11 of 12 patients.
source: We identified 53 such goal-responsive cells (11% of 466 MTL neurons; main effect of goal, p<0.05), which were present in 11 of 12 patients.
evidence: The claim is based on the distribution of goal-responsive cells across patients.

claim: Significant counts of goal-responsive neurons were observed in the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, and premotor cortex.
source: We observed significant counts of goal-responsive neurons in the hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, and premotor cortex (Figure 1B; Binomial tests, p's < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Binomial tests) and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Significant counts of navigational planning neurons were observed in the hippocampus of 9 of 12 patients and in all areas except the amygdala.
source: We observed significant counts of navigational planning neurons in the hippocampus of 9 of 12 patients and in all areas except the amygdala (Figure 1E; Binomial test, p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Binomial test) and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Modulation of firing rate by arrival at goals was observed in parahippocampal and motor areas.
source: Furthermore, we observed modulation of firing rate by arrival at goals in parahippocampal and motor areas (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: 24 cells showed significant interactions between goal and task period (p<0.05).
source: We found 24 cells with significant interactions between goal and task period (p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of neuronal firing data.

claim: The MTL encodes information about navigational goals using modulations in firing rate at the single-neuron level.
source: These results provide single-neuron evidence that the MTL encodes information about navigational goals, and supports navigational planning towards reaching these goals, using modulations in firing rate, extending previous findings (Ekstrom et al., 2003; Watrous et al., 2011; Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on the firing rate data presented in the study and extends prior findings.

claim: The MTL supports navigational planning towards reaching goals using modulations in firing rate at the single-neuron level.
source: These results provide single-neuron evidence that the MTL encodes information about navigational goals, and supports navigational planning towards reaching these goals, using modulations in firing rate, extending previous findings (Ekstrom et al., 2003; Watrous et al., 2011; Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on the firing rate data presented in the study and extends prior findings.

claim: Human MTL oscillations are lower frequency and less stationary compared to the stable theta oscillations observed in rodents.
source: Examining this hypothesis required that we accurately identify the presence and phase of slow oscillations, particularly because human MTL oscillations are lower frequency and less stationary compared to the stable theta oscillations observed in rodents (Watrous et al., 2013; Vass et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MODAL identifies narrow-band oscillations exceeding the background 1/f spectrum.
source: MODAL identifies narrow-band oscillations exceeding the background 1/f spectrum (Figure 2A) and calculates the instantaneous phase and frequency of oscillations in each band (see Materials and methods) while excluding time points without oscillations or that exhibited epileptogenic activity (Gelinas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim describes the MODAL algorithm as developed in the study, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: MODAL calculates the instantaneous phase and frequency of oscillations in each band.
source: MODAL identifies narrow-band oscillations exceeding the background 1/f spectrum (Figure 2A) and calculates the instantaneous phase and frequency of oscillations in each band (see Materials and methods) while excluding time points without oscillations or that exhibited epileptogenic activity (Gelinas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim describes the MODAL algorithm as developed in the study.

claim: MODAL excludes time points without oscillations or that exhibited epileptogenic activity.
source: MODAL identifies narrow-band oscillations exceeding the background 1/f spectrum (Figure 2A) and calculates the instantaneous phase and frequency of oscillations in each band (see Materials and methods) while excluding time points without oscillations or that exhibited epileptogenic activity (Gelinas et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim describes the MODAL algorithm as developed in the study, with citation to prior work on epileptogenic activity.

claim: 93% of MTL electrodes showed a band of activity centered at slow theta (~3 Hz).
source: Analyzing each of 385 LFP channels from the MTL across the entire task period using MODAL, we found that most channels showed a band of activity centered at 'slow theta' (~3 Hz; 93% of electrodes; Figure 2D, gray line).
evidence: The claim is supported by MODAL analysis of LFP data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Slow theta was detected most often across MTL electrodes.
source: Analyzing the overall amount of time each frequency was detected on these electrodes, we found that slow theta was detected most often (Figure 2D, black line).
evidence: The claim is supported by MODAL analysis of LFP data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MODAL can capture multiple narrowband oscillatory signals using a published rodent recording dataset.
source: We then verified that MODAL can capture multiple narrowband oscillatory signals using a published rodent recording dataset (Fujisawa et al., 2008; crcns.org PFC-2 dataset), and observed canonical rodent hippocampal CA1 theta oscillations and a more variable low-frequency rhythm in the medial prefrontal cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by application of MODAL to rodent data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Canonical rodent hippocampal CA1 theta oscillations were observed using MODAL on rodent data.
source: We then verified that MODAL can capture multiple narrowband oscillatory signals using a published rodent recording dataset (Fujisawa et al., 2008; crcns.org PFC-2 dataset), and observed canonical rodent hippocampal CA1 theta oscillations and a more variable low-frequency rhythm in the medial prefrontal cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by application of MODAL to rodent data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A more variable low-frequency rhythm in the medial prefrontal cortex was observed in rodents using MODAL.
source: We then verified that MODAL can capture multiple narrowband oscillatory signals using a published rodent recording dataset (Fujisawa et al., 2008; crcns.org PFC-2 dataset), and observed canonical rodent hippocampal CA1 theta oscillations and a more variable low-frequency rhythm in the medial prefrontal cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by application of MODAL to rodent data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: MODAL is able to identify and track the dynamics of narrowband signals.
source: These results indicate that MODAL is able to identify and track the dynamics of narrowband signals, providing cross-validation for our human findings which are consistent with previous work showing the prevalence of slow theta in the human MTL (Watrous et al., 2011, 2013; Vass et al., 2016; Jacobs, 2014; Bohbot et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on the results from applying MODAL to both human and rodent data.

claim: The prevalence of slow theta in the human MTL is consistent with previous work.
source: These results indicate that MODAL is able to identify and track the dynamics of narrowband signals, providing cross-validation for our human findings which are consistent with previous work showing the prevalence of slow theta in the human MTL (Watrous et al., 2011, 2013; Vass et al., 2016; Jacobs, 2014; Bohbot et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 144 of 466 MTL neurons (30%) showed phase-locked neural firing (Rayleigh test, p<0.005).
source: Across our population of MTL neurons, we identified phase-locked neural firing in 144 neurons (144/466, 30%, Rayleigh test, p<0.005), a proportion significantly above chance (Binomial p<0.00001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Rayleigh test and Binomial test) of spike-phase data.

claim: The proportion of phase-locked neurons (30%) is significantly above chance (Binomial p<0.00001).
source: Across our population of MTL neurons, we identified phase-locked neural firing in 144 neurons (144/466, 30%, Rayleigh test, p<0.005), a proportion significantly above chance (Binomial p<0.00001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Binomial test) of the proportion of phase-locked neurons.

claim: Phase locked neural firing was clustered just after the trough of the oscillation.
source: We observed that phase locked neural firing was clustered just after the trough of the oscillation for these cells (Figure 3B, Rayleigh test p<0.00001) and most phase locking occurred to slow-theta oscillations below 5 Hz (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Rayleigh test) and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Most phase locking occurred to slow-theta oscillations below 5 Hz.
source: We observed that phase locked neural firing was clustered just after the trough of the oscillation for these cells (Figure 3B, Rayleigh test p<0.00001) and most phase locking occurred to slow-theta oscillations below 5 Hz (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Significant counts of phase-locked neurons were observed in each brain region (Binomial test, p<0.0001).
source: Significant counts of phase-locked neurons were observed in each brain region (Binomial test, p<0.0001) and we observed phase-locking most prominently in the hippocampus (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Binomial test) and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Phase-locking was observed most prominently in the hippocampus.
source: Significant counts of phase-locked neurons were observed in each brain region (Binomial test, p<0.0001) and we observed phase-locking most prominently in the hippocampus (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 13.6% of cells (6/44) with two distinct frequency bands showed frequency-specific phase locking.
source: 13.6% of these cells (6/44) showed frequency-specific phase locking, showing phase-locked firing in only one LFP frequency band (Figure 3A; p<0.005 in one band, p>0.1 in all other bands).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of spike-phase data for cells with multiple frequency bands.

claim: 75% of cells with two distinct frequency bands did not show phase-locking to any band or showed phase-locking to both bands.
source: In the remaining cells, 75% did not show phase-locking to any band (n = 33) or showed phase-locking to both bands (n = 5).
evidence: The claim is based on the distribution of phase-locking patterns in cells with multiple frequency bands.

claim: Human neuronal firing can be modulated by the phase of low-frequency oscillations in a band and frequency-specific manner.
source: Thus, extending previous findings (Jacobs et al., 2007) by examining phase-locking to adaptively-identified narrowband signals, we find that human neuronal firing can be modulated by the phase of low-frequency oscillations in a band and frequency-specific manner, as predicted by several models of neural coding (Cohen, 2014; Kayser et al., 2012; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Watrous and Ekstrom, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on the frequency-specific phase-locking data and is consistent with theoretical models.

claim: 63 cells (10% of 627 cells tested) showed individually significant decoding of goal information from spike phases (p<0.05, shuffle corrected).
source: This analysis identified 63 cells (10% of 627 cells tested) across all regions that showed individually significant decoding of goal information from spike phases (p<0.05, shuffle corrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validated decoding analysis of spike-phase data.

claim: The proportion of neurons showing phase coding (10%) exceeded chance levels (Binomial test, p<0.0001).
source: This proportion of neurons exceeded chance levels (Binomial test, p<0.0001) and spike phase coding differentially occurred in the hippocampus (χ2(6)=50, p<0.0001), with 28 of the phase coding cells coming from the hippocampus of nine different patients (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Binomial test) of the proportion of phase-coding neurons.

claim: Spike phase coding differentially occurred in the hippocampus (χ2(6)=50, p<0.0001).
source: This proportion of neurons exceeded chance levels (Binomial test, p<0.0001) and spike phase coding differentially occurred in the hippocampus (χ2(6)=50, p<0.0001), with 28 of the phase coding cells coming from the hippocampus of nine different patients (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) of the distribution of phase-coding cells.

claim: 28 of the phase coding cells came from the hippocampus of nine different patients.
source: This proportion of neurons exceeded chance levels (Binomial test, p<0.0001) and spike phase coding differentially occurred in the hippocampus (χ2(6)=50, p<0.0001), with 28 of the phase coding cells coming from the hippocampus of nine different patients (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is based on the distribution of phase-coding cells across patients.

claim: Roughly half (29/63) of phase coding cells exhibited significant phase-locking (Rayleigh test, p<0.005).
source: Roughly half (29/63) of phase coding cells exhibited significant phase-locking (Rayleigh test, p<0.005), consistent with the idea that phase-locking and phase coding are related but non-identical phenomena (Watrous et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Rayleigh test) of phase-locking in phase-coding cells.

claim: Phase-locking and phase coding are related but non-identical phenomena.
source: Roughly half (29/63) of phase coding cells exhibited significant phase-locking (Rayleigh test, p<0.005), consistent with the idea that phase-locking and phase coding are related but non-identical phenomena (Watrous et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that only half of phase-coding cells show phase-locking, and is consistent with prior work.

claim: 51 (80%) of the cells that showed significant phase coding did not show firing-rate effects (two-way ANOVA, p>0.1).
source: Critically, 51 (80%) of the cells that showed significant phase coding did not show firing-rate effects (two-way ANOVA, p>0.1), indicating that phase coding for a specific goal state can exist independent of firing rate effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) comparing phase-coding and rate-coding cells.

claim: Phase coding for a specific goal state can exist independent of firing rate effects.
source: Critically, 51 (80%) of the cells that showed significant phase coding did not show firing-rate effects (two-way ANOVA, p>0.1), indicating that phase coding for a specific goal state can exist independent of firing rate effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that most phase-coding cells do not show firing-rate effects.

claim: Rate and phase coding each contribute to the neural representation of goals during navigation.
source: These results indicate that rate and phase coding each contribute to the neural representation of goals during navigation.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation of both rate-coding and phase-coding cells in the dataset.

claim: 24 hippocampal neurons showed significant decoding (p<0.05) during the planning period, a proportion significantly above chance (24/186 neurons, 12% Binomial test p<0.00001, chance = 9.3 neurons).
source: We identified a subset of 24 hippocampal neurons that showed significant decoding (p<0.05) during the planning period, a proportion significantly above chance (24/186 neurons, 12% Binomial test p<0.00001, chance = 9.3 neurons).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validated decoding analysis restricted to the planning period.

claim: 24 hippocampal neurons showed phase coding during goal arrival (24/186 neurons, 12%, Binomial test p<0.00001).
source: Similarly, we identified a mostly distinct subset of neurons (e.g., Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2) that showed phase coding during goal arrival (24/186 neurons, 12%, Binomial test p<0.00001).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-validated decoding analysis restricted to the arrival period.

claim: Phase-coding neurons during planning and arrival were largely distinct subsets of hippocampal neurons, with only two neurons significant for both.
source: Importantly, these were largely distinct subsets of hippocampal neurons and were found in different patient groups, with only two neurons significant for both planning and arrival.
evidence: The claim is based on the overlap analysis of phase-coding neurons during planning and arrival.

claim: Phase coding was not observed beyond chance levels in hippocampal cells in the alpha- or beta-band (10–30 Hz) (5.2%, n = 7 of 133 neurons, chance = 5%).
source: Although our primary analysis focused on phase coding to low-frequency (1–10 Hz) oscillations because they were most prevalent in the hippocampus, we also examined whether phase coding was present at the sites that showed alpha- or beta-band oscillations (10–30 Hz). However, we did not observe phase coding beyond chance levels in this population of hippocampal cells in this band (5.2%, n = 7 of 133 neurons, chance = 5%).
evidence: The claim is supported by decoding analysis of spike-phase data in the alpha/beta band.

claim: Phase-coding by individual neurons is specific to particular task periods and frequencies.
source: In sum, we find evidence that phase-coding by individual neurons is specific to particular task periods and frequencies.
evidence: The claim is based on the findings of task-period-specific and frequency-specific phase coding.

claim: Phase coding occurs in distinct hippocampal populations in support of navigational planning and goal arrival.
source: We conclude that phase coding occurs in distinct hippocampal populations in support of navigational planning and goal arrival.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation of distinct phase-coding populations during planning and arrival.

claim: Phase-based coding to slow oscillations is a general phenomenon used by MTL neurons to represent contextual information.
source: More broadly, these findings suggest that phase-based coding to slow oscillations is a general phenomenon used by MTL neurons to represent contextual information.
evidence: The claim is a generalization based on the phase-coding findings in the study.

claim: Average firing rates did not differ between phase-coding and non-phase-coding cells (ranksum test, p=0.39).
source: Average firing rates did not differ between phase-coding and non-phase-coding cells (ranksum test, p=0.39).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ranksum test) comparing firing rates.

claim: Phase coding was not related to the overall prevalence of oscillations detected by MODAL (rho = −0.0049, p=0.9).
source: Phase coding was not related to the overall prevalence of oscillations detected by MODAL (rho = −0.0049, p=0.9) nor to oscillatory bandwidth (rho = 0.008, p=0.85).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between phase coding and oscillation prevalence.

claim: Phase coding was not related to oscillatory bandwidth (rho = 0.008, p=0.85).
source: Phase coding was not related to the overall prevalence of oscillations detected by MODAL (rho = −0.0049, p=0.9) nor to oscillatory bandwidth (rho = 0.008, p=0.85).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between phase coding and oscillatory bandwidth.

claim: The prevalence of oscillations was not modulated as a function of goal in the vast majority (94%) of phase-coding cells.
source: The prevalence of oscillations was not modulated as a function of goal in the vast majority (94%) of phase-coding cells.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of oscillation prevalence across goals in phase-coding cells.

claim: Phase coding for goals is more directly related to coupling between spikes and the LFP than to broader changes in LFP power or spike rates.
source: These results indicate that phase coding for goals is more directly related to coupling between spikes and the LFP than to broader changes in LFP power or spike rates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the control analyses showing no relationship between phase coding and oscillation prevalence, bandwidth, or firing rates.

claim: A significant positive relationship (shuffle corrected p<0.01) was observed between single-neuron firing rate and high-frequency activity in 41% of recorded neurons.
source: Finally, to link these findings to our previous work using high-frequency activity (Watrous et al., 2015a), we observed a significant positive relationship (shuffle corrected p<0.01) between single-neuron firing rate and high-frequency activity in 41% of recorded neurons, suggesting that the phenomena are related in many cases.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between firing rate and high-frequency activity.

claim: Single-neuron firing rate and high-frequency activity are related phenomena in many cases.
source: Finally, to link these findings to our previous work using high-frequency activity (Watrous et al., 2015a), we observed a significant positive relationship (shuffle corrected p<0.01) between single-neuron firing rate and high-frequency activity in 41% of recorded neurons, suggesting that the phenomena are related in many cases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between firing rate and high-frequency activity.

claim: Phase coding is a robust mechanism for neural representation in the human brain during navigation.
source: We thus conclude that phase coding is a robust mechanism for neural representation in the human brain during navigation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the phase-coding findings and control analyses.

claim: The study expands previous observation of phase-coding with high-frequency LFPs to the domain of single neuron spiking.
source: Analyzing recordings from epilepsy patients performing a goal-directed navigation task, we expand our previous observation of phase-coding with high-frequency LFPs (Watrous et al., 2015a) to the domain of single neuron spiking.
evidence: The claim is based on the current study's findings extending prior work.

claim: A distinct population of ~10% of cells showed spike-LFP phase coding in the absence of significant changes in firing rate.
source: In addition to firing rate modulations (discussed below), we found a distinct population of ~10% of cells in which spike-LFP phase coding contributed to representations in the absence of significant changes in firing rate (Hyman et al., 2005; Rutishauser et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on the phase-coding findings in the study.

claim: Neurons were phase-locked to frequency-specific narrowband oscillations primarily in the slow-theta band.
source: In addition, we found neurons that were phase-locked to frequency-specific narrowband oscillations primarily in the slow-theta band.
evidence: The claim is based on the frequency-specific phase-locking findings in the study.

claim: The findings provide new, stronger evidence for SCERT and related models that posit a role for oscillatory phase in neural coding.
source: Together, these findings provide new, stronger evidence for SCERT and related models that posit a role for oscillatory phase in neural coding (Nadasdy, 2009; Kayser et al., 2012; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Watrous and Ekstrom, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on the phase-coding findings supporting theoretical models.

claim: The study replicated the earlier finding of firing-rate coding of goal representations in human single-cell activity.

claim: Rate versus phase coding for goals are partially distinct phenomena.

claim: Neurons may respond maximally to inputs at particular frequencies, likely manifesting as the aggregated LFP signal.
source: This is likely distinct from phase coding at slow frequencies in which both modeling (Cohen, 2014) and empirical studies (Hutcheon and Yarom, 2000; Giocomo et al., 2007) support the idea that neurons may respond maximally to inputs at particular frequencies, likely manifesting as the aggregated LFP signal (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to modeling and empirical studies.

claim: The findings provide the first evidence of phase coding during human navigation.
source: Our findings provide the first evidence of phase coding during human navigation and provide a theoretically important link to other model systems where phase coding is present (Siegel et al., 2009; Kayser et al., 2009; Turesson et al., 2012; Ng et al., 2013), such as phase-precession (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Terada et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on the phase-coding findings in the study and comparison to other model systems.

evidence: The claim is based on the phase-coding findings in the study and comparison to other model systems.

claim: Prominent phase-locking and phase-coding occurred to slower frequency oscillations below 5 Hz.
source: However, we also found prominent phase-locking and phase-coding to slower frequency oscillations below 5 Hz, suggesting that phase coding exists beyond the canonical 8-Hz theta signal seen in rats.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of phase coding at slower frequencies than rodent theta.

claim: (Virtual) navigation-related theta occurs at a slower frequency in humans.
source: These findings thus lend further credence to findings indicating that (virtual) navigation-related theta occurs at a slower frequency in humans (Watrous et al., 2013; Jacobs, 2014; Bohbot et al., 2017) and demonstrates that these oscillations play a functional role in modulating neuronal spiking.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work and the current findings.

claim: Slow theta oscillations in humans play a functional role in modulating neuronal spiking.

claim: The results provide further evidence that the timing of MTL activity is critical for behavior.
source: Our results provide further evidence that the timing of MTL activity is critical for behavior (Reber et al., 2017; Rey et al., 2014).

claim: The goal coding observed in this study reflects flexible coding of spatial contextual information in the service of ongoing behavior.
source: We speculate that the goal coding observed in this study reflects flexible coding of spatial contextual information in the service of ongoing behavior (Warren et al., 2012; Yee et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is presented as speculation based on the findings and prior work.

claim: Both firing rate and the precise timing of activity relative to LFP phase are general coding mechanisms in the human MTL across behaviors and tasks.
source: Combined with previous human studies (Kraskov et al., 2007; Lopour et al., 2013; Watrous et al., 2015a; ten Oever and Sack, 2015), our work indicates that both firing rate and the precise timing of activity relative to LFP phase are general coding mechanisms in the human MTL across behaviors and tasks, suggesting that other types of contextual information may also be encoded using LFP phase.
evidence: The claim is based on the current findings combined with prior human studies.

claim: Other types of contextual information may also be encoded using LFP phase.
source: Combined with previous human studies (Kraskov et al., 2007; Lopour et al., 2013; Watrous et al., 2015a; ten Oever and Sack, 2015), our work indicates that both firing rate and the precise timing of activity relative to LFP phase are general coding mechanisms in the human MTL across behaviors and tasks, suggesting that other types of contextual information may also be encoded using LFP phase.
evidence: The claim is presented as a suggestion based on the generality of phase coding.

evidence: The claim is supported by decoding analysis using HFA events.

claim: The presence of HFA phase coding on a channel was unrelated to the existence of spike-phase coding on the same channel (χ2=0.01, p=0.9).
source: We then asked if the presence of HFA phase coding on a channel correlated with the existence of spike-phase coding on the same channel. However, we found that the presence of these two phenomena were unrelated across channels (χ2=0.01, p=0.9).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) comparing HFA and spike phase coding.

claim: The counter-intuitive result that spike- and HFA-phase coding were not observed on the same channels may reflect a functional heterogeneity of information representation within the human MTL.
source: Thus, while single-neuron firing is correlated with increases in HFA, both of which demonstrate phase coding, spike- and HFA-phase coding were not observed on the same channels. This counter-intuitive result may reflect a functional heterogeneity of information representation within the human MTL, whereby adjacent cells represent different types of information even as they contribute to the same LFP.
evidence: The claim is presented as speculation to explain the unexpected finding.

claim: Adjacent cells in the human MTL may represent different types of information even as they contribute to the same LFP.
source: This counter-intuitive result may reflect a functional heterogeneity of information representation within the human MTL, whereby adjacent cells represent different types of information even as they contribute to the same LFP. This is similar to what has been observed in monkey orbitofrontal cortex regarding the differential information representation shown by single neurons compared to HFA (Rich and Wallis, 2017).
evidence: The claim is presented as speculation based on the findings and is similar to observations in monkey orbitofrontal cortex.
